1.pericope_label: And, behold, there came a man of God out of Judah by the word of the Lord unto Beth–el: and Jeroboam stood by the altar to burn incense. And he cried against the altar in the word of the Lord, and said, O altar, altar, thus saith the Lord; Behold, a child shall be born unto the house of David, Josiah by name; and upon thee shall he offer the priests of the high places that burn incense upon thee, and men’s bones shall be burnt upon thee. And he gave a sign the same day, saying, This is the sign which the Lord hath spoken; Behold, the altar shall be rent, and the ashes that are upon it shall be poured out. And it came to pass, when king Jeroboam heard the saying of the man of God, which had cried against the altar in Beth–el, that he put forth his hand from the altar, saying, Lay hold on him. And his hand, which he put forth against him, dried up, so that he could not pull it in again to him. The altar also was rent, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign which the man of God had given by the word of the Lord. And the king answered and said unto the man of God, Intreat now the face of the Lord thy God, and pray for me, that my hand may be restored me again. And the man of God besought the Lord, and the king’s hand was restored him again, and became as it was before. And the king said unto the man of God, Come home with me, and refresh thyself, and I will give thee a reward. And the man of God said unto the king, If thou wilt give me half thine house, I will not go in with thee, neither will I eat bread nor drink water in this place: For so was it charged me by the word of the Lord, saying, Eat no bread, nor drink water, nor turn again by the same way that thou camest. So he went another way, and returned not by the way that he came to Beth–el.

schools.summary: Ellicott grants the particularity, calling this one of the rather unfrequent prophecies not content to foreshadow the future in general outline but descending to striking detail; but he reports the suggestion that the words Josiah by name are a marginal gloss or an insertion by the chronicler writing after the event, and says of the second that it is in itself not unlikely, before defending the detail on two grounds, that naming a person in prediction is exemplified in the reference to Cyrus and that Josiah means one healed or helped by Jehovah and so is not a mere artificial detail. He shows the identification of the man of God with Iddo impossible from chronology, since Iddo was the chronicler of Abijah's reign and must have lived near the close of Jeroboam's, and suspects the tradition came from a mistaken reading of the visions of Iddo against Jeroboam; and he notes that the English weakens the original, which has the prophet speak not by but in the word of the Lord.

Gill reaches the same verdict on the man's identity from the narrative rather than the chronology, since this man was quickly slain whereas Iddo lived on after Rehoboam and wrote his acts first and last, and he rules out Shemaiah for the same reason although an early writer names him.

Clarke treats the naming of Josiah as among the most remarkable prophecies in the Old Testament, circumstantially foretelling a fact which took place three hundred and forty years after the prediction, and argues its authenticity from the adversarial interest of the parties: the fact was attested by two nations, the Jews guarding most sacredly a prophecy delivered in their behalf and the Israelites, against whom it was levelled, having every interest in exposing its falsehood had that been possible. He supplies the physical detail of the withered arm, that it became suddenly rigid with the nerves no longer communicating their influence and the muscles ceasing to obey the will, and of the altar splitting of its own accord so the ashes were poured out; and he notes that the king says entreat the Lord thy God because Jeroboam knew he was not his own God, being then in the act of acknowledging others.

Henry reads the sending as a mercy rather than a threat, since the army of Judah that aimed to ruin Jeroboam had been countermanded and a prophet was sent instead to reclaim him, and sent in time, while he was only dedicating his altar and before his heart was hardened by the deceitfulness of his sin, for God delights not in the death of sinners. He admires the courage, since those who go on God's errand must not fear the face of man, and notices that the message was addressed neither to Jeroboam nor to the people but to the altar, whose stones would sooner hear and yield than men mad upon their idols; yet in threatening the altar God threatened its founder and worshippers, who might conclude that if his wrath fastens on the lifeless guiltless altar they cannot escape. He turns the prediction into an irony, that the priests of the high places should themselves be the first and only sacrifices on that altar that would please him.

debates: Whether the naming of Josiah belongs to the original prophecy, where Clarke defends it from the adversarial interest of the two nations who preserved and disputed the text, and Ellicott allows that an insertion by the chronicler after the event is in itself not unlikely before defending the detail on other grounds.
Who the man of God was, which Ellicott and Gill agree cannot be Iddo but rule out for different reasons, Ellicott from the dates of the chronicler and Gill from the man's quick death.

What the message was addressed to, which Henry takes to be the altar rather than the king or the people, on the ground that its stones would sooner hear than men mad upon their idols, while the threat still fell on those who built it.
outliers: Clarke notes that the king asks the prophet to entreat the Lord thy God, since Jeroboam knew he was not his own God, being then in the act of acknowledging others.
Ellicott observes that the English weakens the original, which has the prophet speak not by but in the word of the Lord, so that he came clothed in the inspiration of the word put into his mouth.

11.pericope_label: Now there dwelt an old prophet in Beth–el; and his sons came and told him all the works that the man of God had done that day in Beth–el: the words which he had spoken unto the king, them they told also to their father. And their father said unto them, What way went he? For his sons had seen what way the man of God went, which came from Judah. And he said unto his sons, Saddle me the ass. So they saddled him the ass: and he rode thereon, And went after the man of God, and found him sitting under an oak: and he said unto him, Art thou the man of God that camest from Judah? And he said, I am. Then he said unto him, Come home with me, and eat bread. And he said, I may not return with thee, nor go in with thee: neither will I eat bread nor drink water with thee in this place: For it was said to me by the word of the Lord, Thou shalt eat no bread nor drink water there, nor turn again to go by the way that thou camest. He said unto him, I am a prophet also as thou art; and an angel spake unto me by the word of the Lord, saying, Bring him back with thee into thine house, that he may eat bread and drink water. But he lied unto him. So he went back with him, and did eat bread in his house, and drank water. And it came to pass, as they sat at the table, that the word of the Lord came unto the prophet that brought him back: And he cried unto the man of God that came from Judah, saying, Thus saith the Lord, Forasmuch as thou hast disobeyed the mouth of the Lord, and hast not kept the commandment which the Lord thy God commanded thee, But camest back, and hast eaten bread and drunk water in the place, of the which the Lord did say to thee, Eat no bread, and drink no water; thy carcase shall not come unto the sepulchre of thy fathers.

schools.summary: Ellicott denies both halves of that verdict, holding that the narrative implies, and much of its instructiveness depends on it, that the old prophet was neither a pretender to inspiration nor an apostate but one who like Balaam united true prophetic gifts with a low worldliness of temper capable of base subterfuge; he had thrown in his lot with Jeroboam's policy and yet desired to remain a prophet of the Lord. On the deception Ellicott holds the belief culpable, since the falsehood ought to have been obvious to one who had a plain command and was believed only because it chimed in with a secret reluctance to obey and so give up all reward, making the belief self-deceit. On the sentence he finds it the most terrible feature of the history that it is spoken, unwillingly as in the case of Balaam, through the very lips which had lured the prophet of Judah from the right path and at the very table of treacherous hospitality, and complains that Josephus misses the point by assigning the revelation to the prophet of Judah himself; he then generalises the incident into a law, that the voice of worldly wisdom first beguiles the servants of God to disobedience by false glosses on their duty and then proclaims unsparingly their sin and its just punishment.

Clarke takes a third position on the old prophet, that he was once a prophet of the Lord fallen from his steadfastness yet not so deeply as to lose the knowledge of the true God, noting that he was not himself at the king's sacrifice though his sons were; and on the motive he is mildest, saying he can hardly think there was any evil design and that curiosity about the prediction explains it. He floats an exculpation of the man of God, that he permitted himself to be imposed on and might have reasoned that the God who gave the charge had authority to dispense with the rest of it, as with Abraham and Isaac. On the sentence he adopts the escape Ellicott condemns, reporting Kennicott that the original words will bear either he who brought him back or whom he had brought back, and taking the speaker for the voice of God from heaven with the old prophet having nothing to do in the business.

Henry will not soften the old prophet's character, calling him a false prophet and a bad man, since it is easier to believe a confirmation was extorted from a bad character than that a true prophet should tell so deliberate a lie and father it upon God. He supposes the man trained among the sons of the prophets, retaining the name while the spirit of prophecy had departed, and judges the design bad, to draw the man of God into a snare, false prophets having ever been the worst enemies of the true, sometimes aiming to destroy and sometimes to debauch them.

debates: What the old prophet was, where Henry calls him a false prophet and a bad man, Ellicott holds him a man of genuine gifts and worldly temper on the model of Balaam, and Clarke makes him a lapsed but not malevolent prophet of the Lord.

Who pronounced the sentence on the man of God, which Ellicott insists was spoken through the deceiver's own lips and calls the most terrible feature of the history, while Clarke follows Kennicott's grammatical reading to make it a voice from heaven with the old prophet uninvolved.

Whether the man of God was culpable in believing the lie, which Ellicott affirms as self-deceit chiming in with a secret reluctance to obey, while Clarke floats the defence that he might reasonably have thought the charge dispensed with.
outliers: Ellicott generalises the episode into a law, that the voice of worldly wisdom first beguiles the servants of God to disobedience by false glosses on their duty and then proclaims unsparingly their sin and its punishment.
Ellicott complains that Josephus, with his perverse tendency to explain away all that seems startling, assigns the revelation to the prophet of Judah himself and so misses the point.

23.pericope_label: And it came to pass, after he had eaten bread, and after he had drunk, that he saddled for him the ass, to wit, for the prophet whom he had brought back. And when he was gone, a lion met him by the way, and slew him: and his carcase was cast in the way, and the ass stood by it, the lion also stood by the carcase. And, behold, men passed by, and saw the carcase cast in the way, and the lion standing by the carcase: and they came and told it in the city where the old prophet dwelt. And when the prophet that brought him back from the way heard thereof, he said, It is the man of God, who was disobedient unto the word of the Lord: therefore the Lord hath delivered him unto the lion, which hath torn him, and slain him, according to the word of the Lord, which he spake unto him. And he spake to his sons, saying, Saddle me the ass. And they saddled him. And he went and found his carcase cast in the way, and the ass and the lion standing by the carcase: the lion had not eaten the carcase, nor torn the ass. And the prophet took up the carcase of the man of God, and laid it upon the ass, and brought it back: and the old prophet came to the city, to mourn and to bury him. And he laid his carcase in his own grave; and they mourned over him, saying, Alas, my brother! And it came to pass, after he had buried him, that he spake to his sons, saying, When I am dead, then bury me in the sepulchre wherein the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones: For the saying which he cried by the word of the Lord against the altar in Beth–el, and against all the houses of the high places which are in the cities of Samaria, shall surely come to pass. After this thing Jeroboam returned not from his evil way, but made again of the lowest of the people priests of the high places: whosoever would, he consecrated him, and he became one of the priests of the high places. And this thing became sin unto the house of Jeroboam, even to cut it off, and to destroy it from off the face of the earth.

schools.summary: Ellicott supplies natural history on the lion, that lions are mentioned in the Old Testament not unfrequently and especially in southern Palestine and that now the forests have disappeared the lions have disappeared with them. On the old prophet's reaction he is acute, that he did not know how his prediction was to be fulfilled but recognised its supernatural fulfilment at once, and that there is a characteristic reticence about his own share in the business, both the deceit and the prediction, perhaps indicating the strange mixture of remorse and unscrupulous policy that comes out later. On the sequel he draws an inference nobody else notices, that the emphatic tone of whosoever would, he consecrated him possibly indicates that in spite of all Jeroboam could do there was difficulty in finding candidates for the unauthorised priesthood; and he takes the closing verse for the author's own comment, based on the later denunciation by Ahijah.

Clarke reaches the same severity but keeps a mercy Henry does not mention, that the man committed the sin unto death, meaning such a sin as God punishes with the death of the body while extending mercy to the soul. He insists that the roadside scene was preternatural, since the lion though it killed the man does not devour him, the ass stands by unafraid and the lion does not tear the ass, both standing as guardians of the fallen prophet; and he takes the old prophet's request to be buried beside him as arguing a strong conviction that the dead man was holy. On the cities of Samaria he sets out the chapter's historical difficulty squarely, that Samaria was not built at this time since Omri founded it fifty years after Jeroboam's death on a hill bought from a man named Shemer, and offers three answers without finally choosing between them: that the prophet spoke by the spirit of prophecy, calling things that are not as though they were; that the historian added the words because Samaria existed in his own time; or, on Houbigant's solution, that God gave the revelation and the prophet spoke by anticipation.

Henry asks why the death was so severe for so small an offence and answers in two parts. First the offence was great and the lie no excuse, since the man could not be as certain of a countermand sent through another as of the command given to himself and had no ground to think it recalled while its reason remained; he had reason besides to suspect a prophet who did not bear his own testimony against the idolatry of his city, and should have begged direction from God rather than complying at once. Henry presses the excuses in turn, asking whether he thought the old prophet's house safer to eat in than any other at Bethel when God had forbidden him to eat in any, which was to refine upon the command and make himself wiser than God, and whether he pleaded hunger, having never read that man lives not by bread alone. Second the death was for the glory of God, since two things appeared by it, that nothing provokes him more than disobedience to an express command though in a small matter, and that no man is protected in disobedience by the sanctity of his profession or the dignity of his office.

debates: Why the death was so severe for so small an offence, which Henry answers by magnifying the offence and by making the death a demonstration that no office protects a man in disobedience, while Clarke keeps the severity but distinguishes the death of the body from the fate of the soul.

How the cities of Samaria can be named before Samaria was founded, where Clarke sets out the difficulty and offers three solutions - prophetic anticipation, a later historian's phrasing, or revelation spoken by anticipation - without finally choosing.
Whether Jeroboam's priesthood was easily filled, which Ellicott doubts on the strength of the emphatic whosoever would, taking it to indicate difficulty in finding candidates.
outliers: Clarke holds the whole roadside scene preternatural, the lion not devouring the man and the ass standing by unafraid, both as guardians of the fallen prophet.
Ellicott notes that now the forests have disappeared from Palestine the lions have disappeared with them.
